title: The Mystery of the Chalk Arrows
markdown:
Mist curled off the dewy grass of Farmer Giles’s yard. Clove the crow, who loved shiny things and also loved noticing, tilted his head. Across the grey stones lay a chalk arrow, bold and white, too neat to be a child’s scribble.

He had never seen chalk arrows here. A dropped button or a bit of foil would normally have had him diving. This was better than sparkle.

Another arrow appeared a few wingbeats on, pointing the same way. Then another. They seemed to bloom with the dawn, a neat row of tiny fingers toward the far side of the yard.

“What in the crow’s nest,” he muttered.

A blur of dark blue and white dropped from the stable rafters. Pippit the swallow landed on a fence post, wings a whisper. Pippit liked things just so. He would notice a straw out of place, or a web holding dew like tiny beads.

“Clove. The arrows. Peculiar, aren’t they?”

Clove puffed his chest. “A mystery. They’re leading somewhere.”

Together they followed. The first arrow sat by the water trough, where the stones were always dark. The next cut across the ruts the cart made on market days. The trail took them past sleepy shaggy sheep, wool still damp from the night, one ewe lifting her head as if chalk were a kind of grass she had not been offered. They hopped and fluttered around the old oak at the field’s edge, its branches like an old man’s fingers. A bottle cap winked in the roots; Clove almost stooped, then left it. Always the arrows pointed to one place: the top of the farm’s weather vane, a proud rooster with a faded comb that had not spun in years. It stood silent against a vast blue sky.

“They always point to the vane,” Pippit said, circling. “It’s only metal and rust.”

A gruff woof shattered the quiet. Bartholomew, the farm’s big good-natured sheepdog, had spotted them from the dairy door. He was not a bad dog. He simply believed chasing birds was the best game ever, and he had the tail to prove it. Clove and Pippit scattered in a flurry, one over the trough, one along the henhouse roof. Barks and a thumping tail turned the chalk into a blur. White dust lifted. For a moment the clues seemed lost. They needed to finish before playfulness wiped the yard clean.

When they settled on the sun-warm barn roof, ruffled and breathless, Clove nudged Pippit. “Menace. But look.”

The arrows were still there, pointing as steadily as ever, as if Bartholomew’s joy had never happened.

They hopped down to the vane’s stone base. Cool rough rock under their feet. Lichen grew in the joints, pale as old milk. The chalk led right to it, the last arrow a little smudged where a boot or a paw had almost ended the story early. Clove’s eye for tiny things caught what Pippit had missed.

“This brick. Loose.”

He tapped. The stone gave a little wobble. They pecked and nudged. Claws scrabbled. The farmyard seemed to hold its breath. Even Bartholomew stopped barking and watched with his head on one side.

Then the wind picked up. It rattled the oak and made the vane creak. The chalk, so clear a moment ago, began to fade, white powder dusting away with every gust. They worked faster.

With a last heave from Pippit and a forceful peck from Clove, the brick slid free. In the dark cool gap lay a small yellowed roll of paper, tied with string as old as the vane.

They unfurled it carefully, wings still trembling from the wind. The paper smelled of dry stone and old string. The letters were child-like, the ink faint. Children who had stayed on the farm a long time ago, when homes were far away and the days were difficult, had written of missing their families, and of the kindness of the people who looked after them here. Someone had drawn a cow in the margin, and someone else had crossed it out and drawn a better one. A tiny sun, in crayon that had lost most of its colour, smiled in the corner. The last line was simple: May peace always shine like this sun.

The arrows had not been pointing to sweets or foil. They had been pointing to a memory, tucked where weather and dogs could not quite reach.

Clove and Pippit looked at each other. This was not a secret for the whole farm, not something a bark could hold. They pushed the brick home again. The message sat safe in the dark.

Every morning after, when the sun painted the yard gold and pink, the two of them would glance at the still rooster, and the rooster, who never spun, seemed to glance back.
